Green bee-eater (Merops orientalis) undergoes an incubation period of approximately 14 days [ab = approximately 14 days] when eggs are maintained at a constant 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a thermal condition that optimizes embryonic development in this subtropical species. Newly hatched chicks emerge at a remarkably low mass of just 3.153 grams [Wwb = 3.153 grams], reflecting the altricial state typical of coraciiform birds. This minimal starting weight necessitates an intensive period of biparental provisioning, during which the nestlings are fed a diet almost exclusively composed of small hymenopterans. The rapid growth trajectory that follows is fueled by the high frequency of feeding visits, with both parents making dozens of trips daily to the nest burrow. Comparative data from other bee-eater species, particularly the congeneric Merops bullockoides, indicate that this pattern of a very low birth mass followed by a steep growth curve is a conserved life-history strategy within the genus. The developmental timeline is tightly linked to thermal conditions, as the incubation temperature directly influences the rate of yolk absorption and subsequent organogenesis.

A comprehensive field study of a breeding population in Rajasthan provided detailed data on adult body size. The ultimate wet weight, representing the maximum body mass attained by mature individuals, was recorded at approximately 25 grams [Wwi = approximately 25 grams]. This relatively modest adult mass places Merops orientalis among the smaller members of the Meropidae family. The species exhibits no marked sexual size dimorphism, with both males and females converging on this asymptotic mass after the completion of skeletal growth. This adult weight is consistent with the species' aerial insectivore feeding strategy, which favors a lightweight, agile frame capable of prolonged hawking flights. The transition from the neonate mass of approximately 3 grams to the adult mass of 25 grams represents an eightfold increase in body tissue, a substantial investment that must be completed within the first few weeks of life before the fledgling can achieve independence.

Foraging activity and metabolic performance in this species are highly sensitive to ambient temperature. Under the warm conditions typical of the breeding season, characterized by ambient temperatures near 40 °C [T = 40 °C], we observed a suite of key life-history events that unfold in a predictable sequence. Fledging, defined as the age at which young achieve their first sustained flight and depart the nest, occurs at 27 days after hatching [tx = 27 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This milestone marks the end of the obligate brooding period and the beginning of a short post-fledging dependency phase. Attainment of sexual maturity follows considerably later; puberty is reached at 81 days after hatching [tp = 81 days after hatching], a delay that allows for the full mineralization of the skeleton and the refinement of foraging skills necessary for successful breeding at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. Under the same thermal conditions, the first successful reproductive event, corresponding to the laying of the female's first clutch, typically occurs at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C].

The maximum reproduction rate corresponds to 3.5 offspring per year [Ri = 3.5 offspring per year], composed of a clutch of 3 to 4 eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = 3 to 4 eggs per nesting attempt] and a single brood each year [F_R_i = a single brood each year], reflecting the constraints imposed by a relatively short breeding window in the arid and semi-arid habitats they occupy. This annual reproductive output is relatively low compared to many other passerine birds of similar body size, a pattern that aligns with the species' extended parental care period and its reliance on a temporally variable insect prey base. The moderate clutch size is an adaptive trade-off, balancing the energetic demands of incubation and chick-rearing against the need to maintain adult body condition for future breeding attempts. The total annual productivity per female is therefore modest, but the high survival rates of fledglings, facilitated by intensive post-fledging feeding, compensate for this low fecundity.

Maximum recorded longevity in the wild for the closely related white-fronted bee-eater (Merops bullockoides) is 7 years, and available data indicate that Merops orientalis attains a comparable lifespan of approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years] under favorable conditions at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This comparatively long life, which is notable for a bird of such small body mass, is a hallmark of a slow life-history strategy characterized by delayed reproduction and extended parental investment. The species' ability to survive for multiple years allows individuals to accumulate breeding experience, which has been shown to correlate with increased fledging success in older pairs. Population viability models indicate that this longevity is critical for buffering the species against occasional years of poor reproductive output caused by drought or insect prey scarcity. Conservation efforts aimed at preserving the mosaic of open woodland and scrub habitats favored by this species are essential for maintaining the demographic stability of local populations and ensuring the continuation of their distinctive life history.
